All 52 aligned outline summaries state the controlling idea of their spec paragraph (p01-p55), in spec order; the three introduction callouts match no paragraph, as expected.

results.draft_locus: Two Rate Limits on One Friday Evening ¶4
results.quote: Rate-limit scope matters: a budget may apply to an app, a store or another vendor-defined unit, so consumers do not necessarily share one quota.
results.finding: The outliner needed two phrases (the nine consumers; how rate-limit scope works). The spec's controlling idea for p08 joins the platform-side consumer list with a general rule about quota scope, and the draft states that rule as a free-standing principle, two sections before buckets are defined. The same placement is the corroborated flow problem below.

The other two units marked two_ideas hold one idea each: 'Why Platforms Share ¶4' ties Adobe and Shopware to one spectrum ('Shopware draws the same line'), with extension-by-API as its consequence, as p14 declares; 'In Practice ¶2' is one announced pair ('Two decisions carry over'), as p43 declares.

Every unit traces to a supporting claim: intro and friday to S3/S5; why-share to S1; keep-apart to S2; rate-limits to S3; saas to S4; choices and in-practice to S5; one-tenant to S6; stages to S5/S6; wrong to S2-S4; conclusion and questions to S3-S6.

The introduction opens on a puzzling scenario (an order export waiting while the shop keeps selling), not on a definition, history or announcement.
The conclusion explains the opening case and sorts what holds into established, context-dependent and the author's synthesis; it is not a bare summary or a new topic.

p50 synthesizes (pooled, smoothed capacity vs fixed per-caller limits; the merchant controls its own side); p52-p53 give the so-what: owner per caller, order flow first, four vendor questions, buying more is no substitute.
'The order export that waited while the shop kept selling is now explained.' calls back to Introduction ¶1.

The intro reader predicted the incident, why platforms share and how they keep tenants apart, the rate limit at platform and other vendors, the merchant's decisions (budget, one tenant or several, scale, 2027 plan) and failure modes, in roadmap order, with the running Kestrel & Pine case, Eva's order and dated vendor accounts as evidence.

The reader explains why the storefront held (pooled, smoothed capacity; buyers first) and the flow did not (fixed budgets per app/store/customer; ~7 orders a minute), and plans: callers with owners, order flow first, WMS batches, events and bulk instead of full-catalog syncs, test above peak, ask the WMS vendor; 'A bigger plan does not raise the WMS limit.' It omits moving finance to a daily batch, a detail of the expected plan.
The reader gives both conditions for one tenant, the split triggers (legal entity, assortment, operations team), the costs both ways and the PIM and OMS beneath all tenants.

The reader lists the four questions (isolation unit and move/restore alone; limits and their change under load; region; busiest day) and why: each vendor pools the merchant with customers who peak on the same Friday.
